slides.title: The architects of winning teams
slides.subtitle: Five influential coaches. Five perspectives on leadership.

slides.title: Five coaches, five leadership philosophies
slides.subtitle: Different styles, one common challenge: turning individual talent into collective performance.

cards.title: Pep Guardiola
cards.text: Builds positional structure, collective understanding and coordinated decision-making. Analogy: architectural clarity in engineering.

cards.title: Carlo Ancelotti
cards.text: Known for interpersonal intelligence, composure and adapting his approach to different personalities. Analogy: leadership tailored to each engineer.

cards.title: Jürgen Klopp
cards.text: Emphasises energy, emotional connection and collective commitment. Analogy: building an engaged engineering culture.

cards.title: Alex Ferguson
cards.text: Combined long-term team building, discipline and renewal across generations. Analogy: developing sustainable engineering capability.

slides.title: Pep Guardiola: design the system
slides.subtitle: Make the right decisions easier through shared principles.
slides.text: On the pitch, positional play creates structure without prescribing every movement. In engineering, architecture, engineering standards and clear interfaces serve a similar purpose. Lesson for engineering managers: establish guardrails and shared principles so squads can make autonomous decisions without losing alignment.

slides.title: From Guardiola to engineering
slides.subtitle: Translate tactical clarity into engineering effectiveness.

cards.title: Architecture
cards.text: Define boundaries, interfaces and technical principles that reduce unnecessary complexity.

cards.title: Direction
cards.text: Connect technical decisions to business outcomes and strategic priorities.

cards.title: Coordination
cards.text: Help squads integrate their work without creating unnecessary dependencies.

slides.title: Carlo Ancelotti: understand the individual
slides.subtitle: Different people need different kinds of leadership.
slides.text: Ancelotti is associated with calm authority, relationship building and managing strong personalities. Engineers also differ in experience, confidence, ambition and preferred working styles. Lesson for engineering managers: adapt coaching, feedback and delegation to the individual while maintaining consistent expectations.

slides.title: Equality is not identical treatment
slides.subtitle: Fair leadership means giving people what they need to succeed.

columns.title: One-size-fits-all
columns.text: Same level of guidance for everyone. Experienced engineers feel constrained, while developing engineers may lack support.

columns.title: Situational leadership
columns.text: Adjust autonomy, feedback and support to capability, context and individual needs.

slides.title: Jürgen Klopp: create collective energy
slides.subtitle: Performance improves when people believe in the team and their contribution.
slides.text: Klopp's leadership is closely associated with emotional connection, collective intensity and a recognisable team identity. Engineering teams also need a sense of belonging, shared ownership and a common purpose. Lesson for engineering managers: build psychological safety, celebrate collaboration and make the team's contribution visible.
High performance is not simply a collection of talented individuals. It is talent working together toward a shared purpose.
slides.author: A leadership principle

slides.title: Alex Ferguson: build for the future
slides.subtitle: Winning today matters. Building a team that can keep winning matters more.
slides.text: Ferguson's long tenure at Manchester United involved rebuilding squads, developing young players and sustaining high standards across different eras. Engineering organisations also need to renew skills, strengthen succession and avoid dependence on a few key individuals. Lesson for engineering managers: invest in mentoring, knowledge sharing, technical depth and sustainable team structures.

slides.title: Arsène Wenger: make potential visible
slides.subtitle: Great leaders help people become better than they thought possible.
slides.text: Wenger became known for talent development, a long-term football philosophy and attention to professional preparation. Engineers grow when challenging assignments, constructive feedback and learning opportunities are deliberately designed. Lesson for engineering managers: connect individual development plans to real opportunities, not just training courses.

slides.title: The engineering manager's role
slides.subtitle: The analogy is useful because both roles develop people, shape systems and enable performance.

slides.title: Player versus coach, engineer versus manager
slides.subtitle: The manager's value increasingly comes from enabling others.

left.title: Individual contributor
items: Makes decisions within their own scope.

right.title: Engineering manager
items: Builds the conditions for teams to solve problems.
Creates clarity around decisions and ownership.
Measures impact through sustainable team outcomes.

slides.verdict: A manager does not need to make every play. They need to help the team make better plays.

slides.title: The four responsibilities of an engineering coach
slides.subtitle: Translate leadership philosophy into everyday management practices.

cards.title: Set direction
cards.text: Connect business strategy, product outcomes and engineering priorities.

cards.title: Grow people
cards.text: Coach engineers, develop technical leaders and build future capability.

cards.title: Improve the system
cards.text: Remove friction, strengthen engineering practices and clarify ownership.

cards.title: Protect sustainability
cards.text: Balance delivery, quality, operational resilience and engineering health.

slides.title: Balance delivery and development
slides.subtitle: Strong engineering leadership manages both dimensions rather than sacrificing one for the other.

axes.y: Low team health → High team health

slides.title: Turn philosophy into practice
slides.subtitle: Leadership is visible in decisions, routines and the environment teams experience every day.

slides.title: The engineering leadership cycle
slides.subtitle: A repeatable loop for improving team performance.

steps.title: Understand
steps.desc: Assess team health, capability and constraints.

steps.title: Coach
steps.desc: Give feedback, develop skills and delegate decisions.

steps.title: Enable
steps.desc: Remove obstacles and improve the engineering system.

steps.title: Learn
steps.desc: Review outcomes, adapt and improve continuously.

slides.title: Connect coaching to engineering outcomes
slides.subtitle: Translate leadership behaviours into observable signals without reducing performance to a single metric.

slides.title: Build a culture of continuous improvement
slides.subtitle: Like elite teams, engineering organisations improve through deliberate practice.

slides.title: Measure what really matters
slides.subtitle: Good coaches look beyond the scoreboard. Engineering managers should do the same.

slides.title: A balanced engineering scorecard
slides.subtitle: Combine delivery outcomes with the health of the system that produces them.

cards.title: Delivery
cards.text: Lead time, deployment frequency, predictability and progress toward product outcomes.

cards.title: Quality and resilience
cards.text: Change failure rate, recovery time, incidents and operational readiness.

cards.title: People and capability
cards.text: Skill growth, engagement, knowledge sharing and sustainable workload.

slides.title: Avoid the scoreboard trap
slides.subtitle: Metrics should guide improvement, not replace judgement.

columns.title: Measure activity
columns.text: Count commits, tickets and hours without understanding value. This can encourage gaming and local optimisation.

columns.title: Understand outcomes
columns.text: Combine delivery data, quality indicators and team feedback. Use trends to discover problems and improve the system.

slides.text: Your success is not what you can deliver alone. It is what your *team can achieve sustainably* without depending on you for every decision.

slides.title: Your next leadership move
slides.subtitle: Bring the coaching mindset into your next team conversation.

slides.title: A practical 30-day challenge
slides.subtitle: Start with small actions that improve clarity, capability and autonomy.

items.text: Agree on one meaningful team outcome.
Hold individual conversations about strengths and development.
Identify and remove one recurring engineering obstacle.
Delegate one meaningful decision to the team.
Review delivery, quality and team feedback together.

slides.text: The goal is not to create a team that needs a great manager. It is to create a team that becomes great through the environment its manager builds.
slides.author: The engineering coaching mindset

slides.title: Coach the system. Grow the people. Enable the team.
slides.subtitle: The best engineering managers combine strategic clarity, individual development and collective accountability to build teams that deliver lasting value.
